questions.title: CompletableFuture Basics
questions.question: What is CompletableFuture and how do you use it for asynchronous programming in Java?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- CompletableFuture: represents a computation that may complete in the future
- supplyAsync: runs a Supplier asynchronously in ForkJoinPool or custom Executor
- thenApply: transform result (like map)
- thenCompose: chain async operations (like flatMap)
- thenCombine: combine two independent CF results
- allOf: wait for all futures; anyOf: complete when any one completes
- exceptionally / handle: error recovery
- join() vs get(): join() throws unchecked; get() throws checked

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
CompletableFuture represents a computation that may not be done yet. You can start it, attach callbacks that run when it completes, chain multiple async operations together, and combine results from multiple concurrent operations — all without blocking threads.

SupplyAsync starts an asynchronous computation that returns a value. By default it uses the ForkJoin common pool, but you should pass a custom Executor for I/O-bound work to avoid blocking ForkJoin threads. ThenApply transforms the result like a map. ThenCompose is for when your transformation itself is asynchronous — like calling a service that returns a CompletableFuture.

The real power is combining multiple concurrent operations. AllOf lets you wait for multiple independent operations to complete — for example, fetching user data, orders, and preferences in parallel and combining all three once all are done. This is much faster than sequential calls.

speakable_v2.hook: CompletableFuture represents a computation that may not be done yet.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This is much faster than sequential calls.

questions.title: CompletableFuture Patterns and Best Practices
questions.question: What are the key patterns and best practices for using CompletableFuture in a Spring Boot application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Custom thread pool for I/O-bound work — never block ForkJoin common pool
- allOf vs anyOf: allOf waits for all; anyOf completes on first result
- Spring @Async: annotation-based async; same proxy limitation as @Transactional
- join() wraps exceptions in CompletionException — always unwrap for meaningful errors
- orTimeout / completeOnTimeout: set per-future deadline
- Bulkhead pattern: separate thread pools per external dependency
- Don't use in reactive stack (WebFlux) — use Project Reactor instead

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The most important practice with CompletableFuture is using a dedicated thread pool for I/O-bound operations rather than the ForkJoin common pool. The common pool is shared across the JVM and designed for CPU-bound tasks. Blocking it with HTTP calls or database operations will starve other async operations application-wide.

Spring's @Async annotation integrates well — annotate a method and Spring executes it in a configured thread pool. The same self-invocation limitation as @Transactional applies: calling an @Async method from within the same class bypasses the proxy and runs synchronously.

For production resilience, pair CompletableFuture with Resilience4j. You wrap async operations with circuit breakers and rate limiters, applying the same resiliency patterns you'd use for synchronous code.

speakable_v2.cap: You wrap async operations with circuit breakers and rate limiters, applying the same resiliency patterns you'd use for synchronous code.

questions.title: Java Concurrency Essentials
questions.question: What are the core Java concurrency concepts — synchronized, volatile, and atomic classes?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- synchronized: mutual exclusion — one thread at a time; provides visibility too
- volatile: visibility guarantee — no caching in CPU registers; no compound atomicity
- Atomic classes: lock-free CAS operations — AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicReference
- ReentrantLock: tryLock(), timed lock, fairness policy
- ReadWriteLock: concurrent reads, exclusive writes
- happens-before: Java Memory Model guarantee
- ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList: thread-safe collections

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Synchronized ensures only one thread executes a block at a time and provides memory visibility — changes inside a synchronized block are visible to the next thread entering the same lock. The downside is contention: all threads queue for the lock.

Volatile is weaker — it only provides visibility, not atomicity. Reading then incrementing a volatile int is still a race condition because it's three separate operations. For counter operations, use AtomicInteger instead.

AtomicInteger uses CPU-level Compare-And-Swap: if the current value matches what I expected, atomically update it; if not, retry. This gives you thread-safe operations without a lock, making it significantly faster than synchronized for single-variable updates.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Synchronized ensures only one thread executes a block at a time and provides memory visibility — changes inside a synchronized block are visible to the next thread entering the same lock.
speakable_v2.cap: This gives you thread-safe operations without a lock, making it significantly faster than synchronized for single-variable updates.

questions.title: Virtual Threads and Structured Concurrency (Java 21)
questions.question: What are virtual threads in Java 21 and how do they change async programming?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Virtual threads: lightweight JVM-managed threads — millions concurrent; not OS threads
- Platform threads: traditional — backed by OS thread, limited count (~thousands)
- Blocking is fine on virtual threads — JVM unmounts from carrier thread during blocking I/O
- Spring Boot 3.2+: one line to enable virtual threads for Tomcat
- No need for reactive programming for scalability with virtual threads
- Structured Concurrency (preview): StructuredTaskScope — scoped lifetime for subtasks
- Pinning: synchronized blocks pin virtual thread to carrier — prefer ReentrantLock
- Context propagation: MDC, ThreadLocal — use ScopedValue instead (preview)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Virtual threads are Java 21's answer to the scalability challenge that drove teams to reactive programming. Platform threads are backed by OS threads — you can practically run a few thousand before memory and scheduling overhead becomes a problem. Virtual threads are managed by the JVM itself. You can have millions of them. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, the JVM unmounts it from its carrier thread without blocking that carrier thread, so the carrier can run other virtual threads.

This changes the concurrency model fundamentally. With platform threads, blocking I/O wastes a thread — that's why we needed reactive programming and CompletableFuture chains. With virtual threads, blocking I/O is cheap, so you can write straightforward imperative blocking code and get the same scalability as reactive.

For Spring Boot applications, enabling virtual threads is a single property change in Spring Boot 3.2. Each incoming HTTP request gets its own virtual thread instead of a platform thread from Tomcat's pool. The application handles far more concurrent requests without code changes — no reactive refactoring required.

questions.title: Thread Pool Sizing and Executor Configuration
questions.question: How do you size and configure thread pools for a Java backend application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- CPU-bound: pool size ≈ available processors (Runtime.availableProcessors())
- I/O-bound: pool size much larger — threads mostly waiting; Little's Law guides sizing
- Little's Law: throughput = threads / average_latency
- Separate pools per concern: HTTP, DB, external APIs — prevent one slow service from blocking all
- Queue capacity: bounded queues prevent OOM; CallerRunsPolicy for backpressure
- ThreadPoolTaskExecutor: Spring's configurable executor with metrics
- Monitoring: active threads, queue depth, rejection count — expose via Actuator/Micrometer
- Virtual threads (Java 21): bypass sizing concerns for I/O-bound work

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Thread pool sizing depends entirely on the nature of the work. For CPU-bound tasks — computations, parsing, encoding — the optimal pool size is roughly the number of available CPU cores. More threads than cores just adds context switching overhead.

For I/O-bound tasks — HTTP calls, database queries — threads spend most of their time waiting for responses. You can have far more threads than cores because they're not actually using CPU while blocked. A reasonable starting point for I/O pools is 10 to 20 threads, but you should measure under realistic load. The key formula from Little's Law: throughput equals concurrency divided by average latency. If each DB query takes 50ms and you need 200 queries per second, you need at least 10 threads.

In production, I configure separate thread pools for different external dependencies — one for the database, one for each external API. This is the bulkhead pattern. If one external service degrades and its calls take 10 seconds, only that pool fills up. Other operations continue normally instead of the entire application stalling.

questions.title: Async vs Reactive — CompletableFuture vs Project Reactor
questions.question: When should you use CompletableFuture versus reactive programming (Project Reactor / WebFlux)?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- CompletableFuture: imperative, straightforward, good for parallel aggregation
- Project Reactor (Mono/Flux): fully non-blocking, backpressure support, streaming
- WebFlux: reactive web framework — non-blocking from HTTP down to DB (R2DBC)
- Don't mix blocking code in reactive pipelines — blocks event loop
- Virtual threads (Java 21): reduces need for reactive — blocking is cheap again
- Use reactive when: streaming data, real-time push, very high concurrency with I/O
- CompletableFuture fine for: parallel aggregation, occasional async, traditional DB (JDBC)
- Operators: map, flatMap, zip, filter, buffer, window — powerful but complex

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
CompletableFuture and Project Reactor solve different problems. CompletableFuture is great for running a few operations in parallel and combining results — like fetching data from three APIs concurrently. It's familiar, easy to reason about, and integrates naturally with Spring MVC.

Project Reactor and WebFlux are fully non-blocking down the entire stack. When a reactive pipeline is waiting for I/O, the event loop thread is free to handle other requests. This enables handling far more concurrent connections with fewer threads. It also provides backpressure — the consumer can signal how much data it can handle, preventing overwhelming of downstream systems. This is essential for streaming large datasets.

The practical guidance in 2024: if you're on Java 21 with virtual threads, you get most of reactive's scalability benefits without the complexity. Use Spring MVC with virtual threads enabled for most microservices. Reserve WebFlux for use cases where streaming, backpressure, or true non-blocking end-to-end matters — like a real-time notification service or a service that streams large files.
